notes:
1. Meaning of Satyagraha

  • Satyagraha was Mahatma Gandhi's distinctive method of resisting injustice through truth and non-violence.

Gandhi considered it both:

  • A political method
  • An ethical principle
📌 Must-Memorise

Satyagraha → Truth + Non-Violence + Self-Suffering

2. Meaning of the Word

  • Satya means truth.
  • Agraha means firmness, insistence or holding firmly.
  • Satyagraha broadly means holding firmly to truth.

3. Passive Resistance and Satyagraha

  • Gandhi initially encountered the expression passive resistance.
  • He considered it inadequate to describe his method.
  • Satyagraha demanded active moral courage rather than passive submission.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Passive Resistance ≠ Satyagraha

4. Basic Principles

Satyagraha rested on:

  • Truth
  • Non-violence
  • Self-suffering
  • Fearlessness
  • Discipline
  • Willingness to accept punishment

5. Satya

  • Truth formed the foundation of Gandhi's political philosophy.
  • A Satyagrahi was expected to avoid deliberate deception.

6. Ahimsa

  • Ahimsa meant non-violence.
  • Gandhi understood it as more than merely avoiding physical violence.

7. Self-Suffering

  • A Satyagrahi should be willing to suffer rather than deliberately inflict suffering on another person.
📌 Must-Memorise

Satyagraha → Accept Suffering, Do Not Inflict It

8. Acceptance of Punishment

A person deliberately disobeying an unjust law should be prepared to:

  • Face arrest
  • Accept imprisonment
  • Accept legal consequences

9. Moral Appeal

  • Satyagraha attempted to resist injustice while appealing to the conscience of the opponent.

10. Means and Ends

  • Gandhi argued that the means used to obtain freedom were as important as the final objective.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Ethical End → Ethical Means

11. Fearlessness

Satyagraha required courage because participants might face:

  • Police violence
  • Arrest
  • Loss of property
  • Imprisonment

12. Discipline

  • Gandhi repeatedly insisted that a mass movement could succeed only if participants maintained non-violent discipline.

13. Satyagraha and Cowardice

  • Gandhi did not equate non-violence with weakness.
  • He considered disciplined non-violence a form of courage.

14. Open Resistance

  • Satyagraha was generally conducted openly rather than through secret conspiracy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Satyagraha → Open Resistance, Secret Armed Organisation → Chapter 29

15. Negotiation

  • Satyagraha did not reject negotiation.
  • Resistance and negotiation could operate together.

16. Gandhi in South Africa

  • Gandhi developed the basic principles of Satyagraha during his political struggles in South Africa.
📌 Must-Memorise

Origin of Gandhian Satyagraha → South Africa

17. Gandhi Reached South Africa

  • Gandhi travelled to South Africa in 1893.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi → South Africa → 1893

18. Racial Discrimination

Indians in South Africa faced discrimination concerning:

  • Registration
  • Immigration
  • Movement
  • Marriage
  • Taxation

19. Pietermaritzburg Incident

  • Gandhi was removed from a first-class railway compartment at Pietermaritzburg despite possessing a valid ticket.
  • The incident became one of the most famous examples of racial discrimination experienced by Gandhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pietermaritzburg → Gandhi → Racial Discrimination

20. Natal Indian Congress

  • Gandhi helped establish the Natal Indian Congress in 1894.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natal Indian Congress → Gandhi → 1894

21. Early Political Methods

Gandhi initially used:

  • Petitions
  • Legal arguments
  • Public campaigns

  • His political method gradually developed into Satyagraha.

22. Phoenix Settlement

  • Gandhi established the Phoenix Settlement in South Africa in 1904.
📌 Must-Memorise

Phoenix Settlement → 1904

23. Indian Opinion

  • Gandhi used the newspaper Indian Opinion to communicate political ideas and grievances.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Opinion → Gandhi → South Africa

24. 1906 Turning Point

  • The decisive Satyagraha phase began in the Transvaal in 1906.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Satyagraha Campaign → South Africa → 1906

25. Asiatic Registration Law

  • The Transvaal administration introduced compulsory registration requirements targeting Asian residents.

26. Resistance to Registration

  • Indians were expected to register under the discriminatory system.
  • Gandhi organised resistance against compulsory registration.

27. Pledge of Resistance

  • Participants pledged not to submit to the discriminatory law even if they faced imprisonment.

28. Satyagraha Name

  • Gandhi wanted a term different from passive resistance.
  • Satyagraha became the name of the new method.

29. Registration Certificates

  • Resistance included public refusal to accept registration requirements.

30. Burning Certificates

  • Registration certificates were publicly burned as an act of defiance.

31. Arrests

  • Gandhi and many other Indian resisters were repeatedly imprisoned.

32. Jan Smuts

  • General Jan Smuts became one of Gandhi's principal political opponents during the South African campaigns.
📌 Must-Memorise

South African Satyagraha → Gandhi ↔ Jan Smuts

33. Tolstoy Farm

  • Tolstoy Farm was established in 1910 near Johannesburg.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tolstoy Farm → 1910

34. Purpose of Tolstoy Farm

It served as a centre for:

  • Communal living
  • Education
  • Discipline
  • Preparation for Satyagraha

35. Leo Tolstoy

  • The farm was named after Russian writer Leo Tolstoy, whose ideas influenced Gandhi.

36. 1913 Satyagraha

  • Another major phase of South African Satyagraha developed in 1913.

37. Major Grievances

Important issues included:

  • £3 tax on former indentured labourers
  • Restrictions affecting Indian marriages
  • Immigration discrimination

38. Women's Participation

  • Indian women participated actively in the 1913 campaign.
📌 Must-Memorise

South African Satyagraha → Major Women's Participation

39. Workers

  • Indian workers and miners participated in strikes and marches.

40. Mass March

  • Gandhi led workers in a large march during the struggle.

41. Repression

Participants faced:

  • Arrest
  • Imprisonment
  • Economic hardship

42. Indian Relief Act

  • Negotiations contributed to the Indian Relief Act of 1914.
📌 Must-Memorise

South African Satyagraha → Indian Relief Act → 1914

43. Importance of South Africa

South Africa gave Gandhi practical experience in:

  • Mass mobilisation
  • Non-violent discipline
  • Prison resistance
  • Negotiation
  • Constructive community life

44. Gandhi Returned to India

  • Gandhi returned permanently to India in January 1915.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi Returns to India → 1915

45. Gopal Krishna Gokhale

  • Gokhale advised Gandhi to understand Indian conditions before entering major political campaigns.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi's Political Mentor → Gopal Krishna Gokhale

46. Study of India

Gandhi travelled through India and studied:

  • Rural poverty
  • Social conditions
  • Political organisations

47. Kochrab Ashram

  • Gandhi established an ashram at Kochrab near Ahmedabad in 1915.

48. Sabarmati Ashram

  • The ashram later moved to Sabarmati.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sabarmati Ashram → Ahmedabad

49. Ashram Discipline

Followers were trained in:

  • Truth
  • Non-violence
  • Simplicity
  • Manual labour
  • Social equality

50. Local Experiments First

  • Gandhi did not begin immediately with a nationwide movement.
  • His first major Indian struggles dealt with specific local grievances.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Satyagraha Growth → Local → Regional → National

51. Champaran Satyagraha

  • Champaran in Bihar became Gandhi's first major Satyagraha in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran Satyagraha → 1917

52. Main Issue

  • Peasants suffered under exploitative indigo cultivation arrangements imposed by European planters.

53. Tinkathia System

  • The system was known as Tinkathia.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran → Indigo → Tinkathia

54. Tinkathia Meaning

  • Cultivators were traditionally required to grow indigo on three-twentieths of their land.

55. Raj Kumar Shukla

  • Raj Kumar Shukla, a Champaran cultivator, repeatedly requested Gandhi to visit the region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raj Kumar Shukla → Champaran

56. Gandhi Reached Champaran

  • Gandhi went to Champaran in 1917 to investigate peasant grievances.

57. Order to Leave

  • Colonial authorities ordered Gandhi to leave the district.

58. Gandhi's Refusal

  • Gandhi refused to obey the order while accepting the possibility of punishment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Champaran → Civil Resistance to Official Order

59. Court Appearance

  • Gandhi appeared before the authorities and stated that he was prepared to accept punishment.

60. Public Support

  • Large numbers of local peasants gathered in support of Gandhi.

61. Government Retreat

  • The case against Gandhi was withdrawn.
  • He was allowed to continue his investigation.

62. Collection of Evidence

  • Gandhi and his associates recorded evidence from large numbers of cultivators.

63. Rajendra Prasad

  • Rajendra Prasad became an important associate in the Champaran campaign.

64. Brajkishore Prasad

  • Brajkishore Prasad was another important Bihar nationalist involved.

65. J.B. Kripalani

  • J.B. Kripalani was also associated with Gandhi during the Champaran phase.

66. Constructive Work

Gandhi's activity extended beyond indigo grievances to:

  • Education
  • Sanitation
  • Rural welfare
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Champaran → Satyagraha + Constructive Work

67. Inquiry Committee

  • Gandhi became a member of the official committee appointed to investigate agrarian conditions.

68. Settlement

  • The planter system was reformed after investigation and negotiation.

69. Champaran Agrarian Act

  • The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 helped end the Tinkathia system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran → 1917, Agrarian Reform → 1918

70. Importance of Champaran

  • It established Gandhi as a successful mass leader in Indian politics.

71. Ahmedabad Mill Strike

  • Gandhi intervened in a textile labour dispute at Ahmedabad in 1918.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmedabad Mill Strike → 1918

72. Main Issue

  • The dispute centred on wages between mill workers and mill owners.

73. Plague Bonus

  • A major background issue involved the withdrawal or alteration of a plague-related bonus.

74. Workers' Demand

  • Workers demanded a larger wage increase than employers were willing to grant.

75. Gandhi's Advice

Gandhi encouraged workers to:

  • Remain united
  • Avoid violence
  • Maintain discipline

76. Strike

  • Textile workers stopped work.

77. Gandhi's Fast

  • Gandhi undertook a fast during the dispute.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahmedabad 1918 → Gandhi's Fast

78. Settlement

  • Arbitration eventually produced a favourable wage settlement for the workers.

79. Importance of Ahmedabad

  • The Ahmedabad struggle extended Gandhi's method from peasants to industrial workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Champaran → Peasants, Ahmedabad → Workers

80. Kheda Satyagraha

  • Kheda district in Gujarat became another important Satyagraha centre in 1918.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kheda → 1918 → Gujarat

81. Crop Failure

  • Agricultural failure created severe economic distress.

82. Revenue Demand

  • Peasants sought suspension or remission of land revenue.

83. Government Refusal

  • Colonial authorities initially insisted on collection.

84. No-Revenue Resistance

  • Peasants unable to pay were encouraged to collectively refuse payment.

85. Vallabhbhai Patel

  • Vallabhbhai Patel became an important organiser of the campaign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kheda → Gandhi + Vallabhbhai Patel

86. Discipline

Participants were instructed to:

  • Remain united
  • Avoid violence
  • Accept confiscation if necessary

87. Government Concessions

  • Revenue collection was relaxed for poorer cultivators after the agitation.

88. Importance of Kheda

  • Kheda demonstrated the use of disciplined collective revenue resistance.

89. Three Early Indian Experiments

  • Champaran → Indigo cultivators
  • Ahmedabad → Textile workers
  • Kheda → Revenue-paying peasants
📌 Must-Memorise

1917–18 → Champaran + Ahmedabad + Kheda

90. Expansion of Gandhi's Social Base

These struggles connected Gandhi with:

  • Peasants
  • Workers
  • Regional Congress organisers

91. Rowlatt Committee

  • The British government appointed a committee under Justice Sidney Rowlatt to investigate revolutionary activity.

92. Rowlatt Act

  • Repressive legislation based on the committee's recommendations was enacted in 1919.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rowlatt Act → 1919

93. Nature of Rowlatt Legislation

  • It enabled exceptional restrictions including detention without normal safeguards of trial.

94. Gandhi's Opposition

  • Gandhi regarded the legislation as an attack on civil liberties.

95. Satyagraha Sabha

  • Gandhi organised the Satyagraha Sabha to resist the Rowlatt legislation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Satyagraha Sabha → Rowlatt Act

96. First All-India Satyagraha

  • The Rowlatt campaign became Gandhi's first major attempt at nationwide Satyagraha.
📌 Must-Memorise

First All-India Gandhian Satyagraha → Rowlatt, 1919

97. Hartal

  • Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal.

98. 6 April 1919

  • 6 April 1919 became the principal date associated with the Rowlatt hartal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rowlatt Hartal → 6 April 1919

99. Forms of Protest

  • Shops closed.
  • Public meetings were organised.
  • Processions occurred in several cities.

100. Breakdown of Discipline

  • Violence occurred in some places despite Gandhi's instructions.

101. Punjab

  • Punjab became one of the main centres of colonial repression.

102. Saifuddin Kitchlew

  • Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew was a prominent nationalist leader at Amritsar.

103. Dr. Satyapal

  • Dr. Satyapal was another important Amritsar leader.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amritsar 1919 → Kitchlew + Satyapal

104. Arrest of Local Leaders

  • Kitchlew and Satyapal were arrested and removed from Amritsar.

105. Jallianwala Bagh

  • On 13 April 1919, troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired on a gathering at Jallianwala Bagh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jallianwala Bagh → 13 April 1919

106. Political Impact

  • The massacre profoundly damaged Indian faith in British justice.

107. Suspension of Rowlatt Satyagraha

  • Gandhi suspended the movement after violence occurred.

108. Himalayan Miscalculation

  • Gandhi later described the premature launching of mass resistance without adequate non-violent preparation as a "Himalayan miscalculation."
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rowlatt → Lesson in Mass Discipline

109. Lesson from Rowlatt

  • Popular anger alone was insufficient for Gandhi.

Satyagraha required:

  • Training
  • Discipline
  • Self-control

110. Punjab Wrongs

  • British repression in Punjab became one of the major grievances feeding the next phase of the national movement.

111. Khilafat Issue

  • Indian Muslim leaders protested the post-war treatment of the Ottoman Caliphate.

112. Ali Brothers

  • Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali became major Khilafat leaders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ali Brothers → Mohammad Ali + Shaukat Ali

113. Gandhi and Khilafat

  • Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause as part of wider anti-colonial mobilisation and Hindu-Muslim cooperation.

114. Non-Cooperation Movement

  • Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation programme in 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Cooperation Movement → 1920

115. Main Background

The movement united grievances concerning:

  • Punjab repression
  • Khilafat
  • Swaraj

116. Special Calcutta Session

  • Congress approved Non-Cooperation at a Special Session in Calcutta in September 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Special Calcutta Session 1920 → Non-Cooperation Approved

117. Lala Lajpat Rai

  • Lala Lajpat Rai presided over the Special Calcutta Session.

118. Nagpur Congress

  • Congress ratified and consolidated the programme at Nagpur in December 1920.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagpur 1920 → Non-Cooperation Consolidated

119. Congress Reorganisation

  • Congress was reorganised to function as a broader mass political organisation.

120. Linguistic Provinces

  • Provincial Congress Committees were reorganised largely on linguistic lines.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nagpur 1920 → Congress Organisational Reorganisation

121. Membership Expansion

  • Congress membership became more accessible to ordinary people.

122. Programme of Non-Cooperation

It included:

  • Surrender of titles
  • Boycott of government schools
  • Boycott of courts
  • Boycott of legislative councils
  • Boycott of foreign cloth
  • Promotion of khadi

123. National Education

  • National schools and colleges were promoted as alternatives to colonial institutions.

124. Lawyers

  • Several nationalist lawyers reduced or abandoned practice in colonial courts.

125. Students

  • Students withdrew from government-controlled institutions.

126. Foreign Cloth Boycott

  • Boycott of imported cloth linked nationalist politics with daily economic behaviour.

127. Khadi

  • Khadi became one of the most recognisable symbols of Gandhian nationalism.

128. Charkha

The spinning wheel symbolised:

  • Swadeshi
  • Self-reliance
  • Constructive work

129. Mass Participation

Non-Cooperation drew:

  • Students
  • Traders
  • Peasants
  • Workers
  • Women into nationalist politics

130. Local Grievances

  • Different regions joined the movement for different local reasons.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

National Programme + Local Grievances → Mass Expansion

131. Moplah Rebellion

  • The Moplah uprising occurred in Malabar in 1921.
  • It developed from a complicated mixture of agrarian and religious tensions.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Moplah Rebellion ≠ Standard Gandhian Satyagraha

132. Prince of Wales Boycott

  • The Prince of Wales visit in 1921 was boycotted in several places.

133. Chauri Chaura

  • Chauri Chaura became the decisive turning point in the Non-Cooperation Movement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauri Chaura → 5 February 1922

134. Violence at Chauri Chaura

  • Protesters clashed with police.
  • A police station was burned.

135. Police Deaths

  • Twenty-two policemen were killed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauri Chaura → 22 Policemen Killed

136. Gandhi's Decision

  • Gandhi concluded that the movement had lost the required non-violent discipline.

137. Withdrawal

  • Non-Cooperation was suspended in February 1922.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Cooperation Withdrawn → Chauri Chaura

138. Bardoli Meeting

  • The Congress Working Committee at Bardoli approved suspension of the planned mass campaign.

139. Opposition to Withdrawal

  • Several nationalist leaders believed the movement should have continued.

140. Gandhi's Position

  • Gandhi placed non-violence above immediate political advantage.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

For Gandhi → Non-Violence Was a Principle, Not Merely a Tactic

141. Gandhi Arrested

  • Gandhi was arrested in March 1922.

142. Sedition Trial

  • Gandhi was prosecuted for sedition and sentenced to imprisonment.

143. Constructive Programme

  • After the withdrawal, Gandhi placed greater emphasis on constructive work.

144. Main Constructive Activities

These included:

  • Khadi
  • Village industries
  • Hindu-Muslim unity
  • Removal of untouchability
  • Rural reconstruction

145. Purpose

  • Gandhi believed social reconstruction was essential preparation for future mass action.

146. Swarajists

  • C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru favoured entering colonial legislatures and obstructing them from within.

147. No-Changers

Other Congress leaders favoured continuing:

  • Constructive work
  • Council boycott
📌 Must-Memorise

Swarajists → Council Entry, No-Changers → Constructive Programme

148. Bardoli Satyagraha

  • Bardoli in Gujarat became the site of a highly disciplined peasant Satyagraha in 1928.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bardoli Satyagraha → 1928

149. Revenue Increase

  • Peasants opposed an increase in land-revenue assessment.

150. Vallabhbhai Patel

  • Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli movement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bardoli → Vallabhbhai Patel

151. Collective Resistance

  • Peasants collectively refused payment of the enhanced revenue.

152. Non-Violent Discipline

  • Patel insisted on strict discipline and unity.

153. Women's Participation

  • Women played an important role in sustaining the Bardoli campaign.

154. Title Sardar

  • Patel became widely known as Sardar in connection with the success of Bardoli.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bardoli → "Sardar" Patel

155. Historical Significance

  • Bardoli restored confidence in disciplined peasant Satyagraha after the 1922 setback.

156. Lahore Congress

  • Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session of Congress in December 1929.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lahore Congress → 1929 → Jawaharlal Nehru

157. Purna Swaraj

  • Congress adopted complete independence, or Purna Swaraj, as its objective.
📌 Must-Memorise

Purna Swaraj → Lahore Congress

158. Independence Day

  • 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day.
📌 Must-Memorise

26 January 1930 → Purna Swaraj Day

159. Civil Disobedience Authorised

  • Congress authorised Gandhi to launch a new campaign of Civil Disobedience.

160. Gandhi's Demands

  • Gandhi communicated a series of political and economic demands to the Viceroy before beginning the movement.

161. Lord Irwin

  • Lord Irwin was Viceroy when the Civil Disobedience Movement began.
📌 Must-Memorise

Civil Disobedience 1930 → Lord Irwin

162. Selection of Salt

  • Gandhi selected the salt tax and government salt monopoly as the central issue.

163. Why Salt?

  • Salt was used by every section of society.
  • A tax on salt affected rich and poor alike.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Salt → Universal Everyday Symbol of Colonial Rule

164. Dandi March

  • Gandhi began the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dandi March Begins → 12 March 1930

165. Initial Satyagrahis

  • Gandhi began the march with 78 selected companions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dandi March → Gandhi + 78 Initial Satyagrahis

166. Destination

  • The march travelled from Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi.

167. Distance

  • The march covered roughly 385 kilometres.

168. Village Mobilisation

  • Gandhi addressed villagers throughout the march.

169. Purpose of March

The march:

  • Publicised Purna Swaraj
  • Mobilised rural communities
  • Challenged the salt monopoly

170. Dandi

  • Gandhi reached Dandi in early April 1930.

171. Salt Law Violation

  • On 6 April 1930, Gandhi symbolically violated the salt law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dandi → Salt Law Broken → 6 April 1930

172. Nationwide Expansion

  • Salt-law violation spread to many regions.

173. Civil Disobedience Beyond Salt

The movement included:

  • Salt manufacture
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Revenue resistance
  • Forest-law violations

174. Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

  • C. Rajagopalachari organised the major Salt Satyagraha march in the Madras Presidency.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Salt Satyagraha → Rajaji

175. Destination

  • The march proceeded to Vedaranyam on the Tamil coast.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajaji → Vedaranyam

176. Starting Point

  • It began from Tiruchirappalli.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vedaranyam March → Tiruchirappalli → Vedaranyam

177. Date

  • The march began on 13 April 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vedaranyam March Begins → 13 April 1930

178. Sardar A. Vedaratnam

  • Sardar A. Vedaratnam was an important local organiser of the Vedaranyam campaign.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Sardar Vedaratnam → Vedaranyam

179. Agasthiyampalli

  • Salt-law defiance took place in the coastal salt-producing area near Agasthiyampalli.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Agasthiyampalli → Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

180. Rukmini Lakshmipathi

  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi was a prominent woman nationalist associated with the Civil Disobedience and Salt Satyagraha period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rukmini Lakshmipathi → Salt/Civil Disobedience

181. Tamil Nadu Participation

  • The Vedaranyam campaign spread Civil Disobedience through parts of the Madras Presidency.

182. Dandi vs Vedaranyam

  • Dandi → Gandhi → Gujarat
  • Vedaranyam → Rajaji → Tamil Nadu
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Gandhi → Dandi, Rajaji → Vedaranyam

183. Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan

  • Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan led a powerful non-violent movement in the North-West Frontier Province.

184. Khudai Khidmatgar

  • His organisation was called Khudai Khidmatgar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khudai Khidmatgar → Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan

185. Red Shirts

  • Its members were popularly known as Red Shirts.

186. Qissa Khwani Bazaar

  • Severe colonial repression occurred at Qissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar in April 1930.
📌 Must-Memorise

Qissa Khwani Bazaar → Peshawar → 1930

187. Frontier Non-Violence

  • The movement demonstrated disciplined non-violent resistance among Pashtun communities.

188. Forest Satyagraha

  • In several regions, protesters violated restrictive colonial forest laws.

189. Peasant Participation

  • Revenue resistance occurred in several agrarian areas.

190. Women in Civil Disobedience

  • Civil Disobedience greatly increased women's direct participation in national politics.
📌 Must-Memorise

Civil Disobedience → Major Women's Participation

191. Women's Activities

Women participated in:

  • Salt manufacture
  • Picketing
  • Processions
  • Boycott
  • Jail-going

192. Sarojini Naidu

  • Sarojini Naidu became an important leader during the Salt Satyagraha phase.

193. Gandhi's Arrest

  • Gandhi was arrested in May 1930 before he could lead the planned action against Dharasana Salt Works.

194. Abbas Tyabji

  • Abbas Tyabji initially took responsibility for leading the Dharasana campaign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dharasana → Abbas Tyabji + Sarojini Naidu

195. Abbas Tyabji Arrested

  • Tyabji was also arrested.

196. Sarojini Naidu at Dharasana

  • Sarojini Naidu became one of the principal leaders associated with the subsequent protest.

197. Police Violence

  • Non-violent volunteers faced severe police beating without armed retaliation.

198. Webb Miller

  • American journalist Webb Miller reported the repression to the international press.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dharasana → Webb Miller

199. International Impact

  • Reports from Dharasana damaged British claims of moral legitimacy.

200. Gandhi–Irwin Negotiations

  • Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin entered negotiations in early 1931.

201. Gandhi–Irwin Pact

  • The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhi–Irwin Pact → 5 March 1931

202. Congress Agreement

  • Congress agreed to suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement.

203. Round Table Conference

  • Gandhi agreed to participate in the Second Round Table Conference.

204. Government Concessions

Important concessions included:

  • Release of many political prisoners not convicted of violence.
  • Permission for peaceful picketing
  • Limited concessions concerning salt manufacture

205. Bhagat Singh Trap

  • The Gandhi–Irwin Pact did not secure commutation of the death sentences of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Gandhi–Irwin Pact ≠ Bhagat Singh Released

206. Karachi Congress

  • Congress met at Karachi in March 1931.

207. President

  • Vallabhbhai Patel presided over the Karachi session.
📌 Must-Memorise

Karachi Congress 1931 → Vallabhbhai Patel

208. Fundamental Rights Resolution

  • The Karachi session adopted an important resolution on Fundamental Rights.

209. National Economic Programme

  • It also adopted a resolution concerning a National Economic Programme.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karachi 1931 → Fundamental Rights + Economic Programme

210. Second Round Table Conference

  • Gandhi travelled to London for the Second Round Table Conference in 1931.

211. Congress Representation

  • Gandhi was the sole official Congress representative at the conference.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Round Table Conference → Gandhi

212. Major Disputes

Differences remained over:

  • Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes because he believed they would permanently divide Hindu society.

  • Gandhi opposed fascism but also rejected Britain's right to involve unfree India in war without consent.

  • Gandhi continued to call for disciplined non-violent mass resistance.

258. South Africa

259. Champaran

260. Ahmedabad

263. Non-Cooperation Movement

264. Bardoli

  • Disciplined regional peasant resistance showed the continued effectiveness of Satyagraha.

265. Civil Disobedience Movement

  • Satyagraha developed into deliberate nationwide law-breaking.

266. Individual Satyagraha

  • Gandhi used limited resistance during wartime.

267. Quit India Movement

The broad progression was:

  • Gandhi drew peasants, workers, women and students more deeply into nationalist politics.

Gandhi connected politics with:

  • Salt

  • Social behaviour

Satyagraha:

Satyagraha:

Non-Cooperation:

Civil Disobedience:

  • Gandhi maintained that non-violent discipline was fundamental to Satyagraha.
